query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor boron microalloying (e.g., ~0.5 wt.% B) to the CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy will promote in situ formation of a continuous, self‐adaptive boron-enriched oxide glaze during sliding that both strengthens the matrix via lattice distortion and continuously renews a lubricious protective layer across the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C, thereby lowering both friction coefficient and wear rate relative to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Pure CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy fabricated by conventional methods (e.g., casting or powder metallurgy) exhibiting moderate hardness, but suffering from unstable friction and wear when tested over a broad temperature range.
generation.intervention: Integrate a low concentration (~0.5 wt.%) of boron into the CoCrFeNi alloy during synthesis.
generation.conditions: Dry sliding tests under controlled loads (e.g., 20–50 N) in ambient atmosphere while systematically varying temperature from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The boron microalloying is expected to induce subtle lattice distortions and, more critically, enhance the formation of a continuous boron-enriched oxide (or borosilicate) glaze on the worn surface.
generation.mechanism: The added boron increases hardness through solid-solution strengthening and simultaneously lowers the activation energy for oxidation in its vicinity. During friction, a stable, thin glaze layer enriched in boron oxides forms in situ. This glaze acts as a self-healing, low shear-strength interface that limits adhesive and abrasive wear, remaining effective over a wide temperature span.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy, the boron-doped version is predicted to exhibit a reduction in the average coefficient of friction (by roughly 20–30%) and a similarly improved wear rate (potentially reduced by around 50% or more) consistently from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics of the unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, which in prior evaluations show relatively high and variable friction coefficients and higher wear rates especially at the high end of the temperature range.
generation.boundary: This study applies to dry sliding conditions in ambient air with temperatures ranging from room temperature (~25 °C) up to 800 °C under moderate load levels. The alloy processing route should enable a homogeneous distribution of the boron without forming brittle secondary phases.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extends findings from studies on boron microalloying in more complex HEA systems (e.g., AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx as reported in PMC12565319) and the concept of adaptive friction interface protection observed in multi-phase alloys (PMC10241162) to the simpler, pure CoCrFeNi matrix. The novelty lies in applying a minimal boron addition to directly achieve both structural strengthening and in situ tribolayer formation within a CoCrFeNi alloy—a gap not yet explored directly over a full temperature range.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi alloy samples using an identical processing route—one set doped with ~0.5 wt.% boron and one undoped as the control. Perform systematic dry ball-on-disk sliding tests under identical conditions (fixed normal load, sliding speed, and test durations) across a series of temperatures (room temperature, 150 °C, 300 °C, 600 °C, and 800 °C). Post-test analysis should include measurement of friction coefficient over time, wear rates (e.g., wear scar depth/volume), and microstructural examination of the worn surfaces (using SEM/EDS) for evidence of a continuous boron-rich glaze layer.
measurements: Average and standard deviation of friction coefficients at each temperature
Cross-sectional and surface microstructural analysis (SEM, EDS, possibly TEM) to verify the presence, continuity, and chemical composition of the formed glaze layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped CoCrFeNi samples do not consistently show statistically significant reductions (e.g., at least a 20% lower mean friction coefficient and markedly reduced wear rate across all test temperatures) compared to the undoped controls, or if no continuous boron-rich oxide layer is observed on the worn surfaces, the hypothesis that minor boron addition confers adaptive, wear-reducing tribolayer formation in CoCrFeNi would be falsified.

High hardness and good wear resistance have been revealed for the high-entropy alloy (HEA) system AlCoCrFeNiTi, confirming the potential for surface protection applications. Detailed studies to investigate the microstructure and phase formation have been carried out using different production routes. Powder metallurgical technologies allow for much higher flexibility in the customisation of materials compared to casting processes. Particularly, spark plasma sintering (SPS) enables the fast processing of the feedstock, the suppression of grain coarsening and the production of samples with a low porosity. Furthermore, solid lubricants can be incorporated for the improvement of wear resistance and the reduction of the coefficient of friction (COF). This study focuses on the production of AlCoCrFeNiTi composites comprising solid lubricants. Bulk materials with a MoS2 content of up to 15 wt % were produced. The wear resistance and COF were investigated in detail under sliding wear conditions in ball-on-disk tests at room temperature and elevated temperature.
